H1.text: A candle under a glass goes out. A rocket carries its own oxygen into space. A stove flame burns gas, quietly using up the air.

H2.text: Every flame eats oxygen. But how much? Chemistry can tell you, to the gram.

H3.text: Aarav watches the stove in his kitchen. His family cooks on natural gas, which is mostly methane.

H4.text: He wonders, how much oxygen does each gram of that gas use up?

H5.text: By the end of this video, you will read any equation like a recipe, in moles, grams and litres.

P1.text: First, what is a chemical equation?

P2.text: It is a short way to write a reaction. Reactants, the starting substances, go on the left.

P3.text: Products, the new substances, go on the right. The arrow means gives.

P4.text: Small letters in brackets tell the state. g for gas, l for liquid, s for solid, and a q for dissolved in water.

P5.text: And stoichiometry is the maths of these amounts. The word comes from two Greek words. Stoicheion means element, and metron means measure.

S1.text: Let's burn methane on our molecule bench. One carbon atom holds four hydrogen atoms.

S2.text: Oxygen gas is two oxygen atoms, joined by two shared pairs of electrons.

S3.text: As written, methane plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide plus water.

S4.text: Watch. The old bonds break, the atoms move, and new bonds form.

S5.text: Carbon takes two oxygens. Hydrogen pairs up with oxygen to make water.

B1.text: Now check the counter. Carbon, one and one. Hydrogen, four and two. Oxygen, two and three. Not balanced.

D1.text: Let's balance it, one atom at a time.

D2.text: Step one. Carbon is already equal. One on each side.

D3.text: Step two. Methane has four hydrogens. Each water holds two. So put a two in front of water. Hydrogen is now four and four.

D4.text: Step three. Now count oxygen on the right. Two in carbon dioxide, plus two in the waters. Four.

D5.text: So we need two oxygen molecules on the left. Put a two in front of oxygen. Oxygen, four and four.

D6.text: Count again. Carbon one, hydrogen four, oxygen four, on both sides. Balanced.

R1.text: Now read the balanced equation like a recipe.

R2.text: In moles. One mole of methane reacts with two moles of oxygen. It gives one mole of carbon dioxide and two moles of water.

R3.text: In grams. Methane is sixteen grams per mole. Oxygen, thirty two. Carbon dioxide, forty four. Water, eighteen.

R4.text: So sixteen grams of methane burns with sixty four grams of oxygen, and gives forty four grams of carbon dioxide and thirty six grams of water.

R5.text: Check. Sixteen plus sixty four is eighty. Forty four plus thirty six is eighty. Mass is conserved.

R6.text: In litres. For gases at S T P, one mole fills twenty two point seven litres. So twenty two point seven litres of methane needs forty five point four litres of oxygen.

B2.text: Look at the two ratios side by side. In moles, one to two. In grams, sixteen to sixty four.

B3.text: Pause and think. One mole of methane needs two moles of oxygen. So does one gram of methane need two grams of oxygen?

B4.text: No! It needs four grams. An oxygen molecule is twice as heavy as a methane molecule. Equations count moles, not grams.

M1.text: Many reactions happen in water, in solutions. There, we count moles using concentration.

M2.text: Your NCERT book gives four ways. Mass percent, mole fraction, molarity and molality.

M3.text: The most used is molarity. Molarity is the moles of solute in one litre of solution.

M4.text: NCERT's example. Four grams of sodium hydroxide, in two hundred fifty millilitres of solution.

M5.text: Sodium hydroxide is forty grams per mole, so four grams is zero point one mole.

M6.text: Zero point one mole in zero point two five litres gives zero point four moles per litre. We write zero point four M.

T1.text: Remember this. A balanced equation is a recipe written in moles.

W1.text: Now, Aarav's question as a worked example.

W2.text: How much oxygen burns four grams of methane? And how much water forms?

W3.text: First, grams to moles. Four grams divided by sixteen is zero point two five moles of methane.

W4.text: The recipe says two moles of oxygen for every mole of methane. So zero point five moles of oxygen. That is sixteen grams.

W5.text: Water is also two to one. Zero point five moles of water, which is nine grams.

W6.text: So four grams of methane uses up sixteen grams of oxygen. Four times its own mass!

X2.text: Some students start calculating straight from the unbalanced equation. Then one methane seems to need only one oxygen.

X3.text: That halves the answer. Always balance first, then use the big numbers in front as your mole ratio.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As mass to mass numericals from a balanced equation, and as molarity calculations.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Propane, C three H eight, burns in oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water. What mass of oxygen is needed to burn eleven grams of propane? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is C. Forty grams.

A2.text: Balance first. C three H eight plus five O two gives three C O two plus four H two O.

A3.text: Propane is forty four grams per mole, so eleven grams is zero point two five moles.

A4.text: Five times that is one point two five moles of oxygen. Times thirty two is forty grams. B used sixteen, the mass of one oxygen atom.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. In the burning of methane, what is the mole ratio of methane to oxygen?

Y3.text: Two. Why does one gram of methane not need two grams of oxygen?

Y4.text: Three. What is the molarity of two grams of sodium hydroxide in five hundred millilitres of solution?

N1.text: Next time: what if the oxygen runs out before the gas does? We find out in limiting reagent.
